# Deploy MCP servers to Vercel

Deploy your Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers on Vercel to [take advantage of features](https://vercel.com/docs/mcp/deploy-mcp-servers-to-vercel#deploy-mcp-servers-efficiently) like [Vercel Functions](https://vercel.com/docs/functions), [OAuth](https://vercel.com/docs/mcp/deploy-mcp-servers-to-vercel#enabling-authorization), and [efficient scaling](https://vercel.com/docs/fluid-compute) for AI applications.

- Get started with deploying MCP servers on Vercel
- Learn how to enable authorization to secure your MCP server
- Add your MCP server to an agent built with AI SDK, eve, or TanStack AI

Vercel provides the following features for production MCP deployments:

- Optimized cost and performance: [Vercel Functions](https://vercel.com/docs/functions) with [Fluid compute](https://vercel.com/docs/fluid-compute) handle MCP servers' irregular usage patterns (long idle times, quick message bursts, heavy AI workloads) through [optimized concurrency](https://vercel.com/docs/fundamentals/what-is-compute#optimized-concurrency), [dynamic scaling](https://vercel.com/docs/fundamentals/what-is-compute#dynamic-scaling), and [instance sharing](https://vercel.com/docs/fundamentals/what-is-compute#compute-instance-sharing). You only pay for compute resources you actually use with minimal idle time.
- [Instant Rollback](https://vercel.com/docs/instant-rollback): Quickly revert to previous production deployments if issues arise with your MCP server.
- [Preview deployments with Deployment Protection](https://vercel.com/docs/deployment-protection): Secure your preview MCP servers and test changes safely before production
- [Vercel Firewall](https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-firewall): Protect your MCP servers from malicious attacks and unauthorized access with multi-layered security
- [Rolling Releases](https://vercel.com/docs/rolling-releases): Gradually roll out new MCP server deployments to a fraction of users before promoting to everyone

Use [`mcp-handler`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/mcp-handler) to create an MCP server in an existing Next.js App Router application. You'll need Node.js 22 or later.

Install `mcp-handler` v2, the MCP server SDK v2, and Zod v4:

Create a route that exposes a tool for rolling an N-sided die:

Clients connect to `/api/mcp` using Streamable HTTP. Your framework determines the route, so you don't need to configure a base path in `mcp-handler`.

Start your Next.js development server at `http://localhost:3000`, then run the [MCP Inspector](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/tools/inspector) with your server's URL:

The Inspector opens in your browser. If it doesn't, open the URL printed in your terminal, which includes a session token.

1. Under Servers, turn on the switch for `localhost:3000` to connect.
2. Select Tools at the top of the page, then select `roll_dice`.
3. Enter a value for `sides`, such as `6`, and select Execute Tool. The result shows the number you rolled.

To check the server from a script or CI job instead, use the Inspector's CLI mode:

When you deploy your application on Vercel, you'll get a URL such as `https://my-mcp-server.vercel.app`.

Add your deployed server's full URL, such as `https://my-mcp-server.vercel.app/api/mcp`, to an MCP host. Claude and ChatGPT connect from their own infrastructure, so use your deployment's URL rather than `localhost`.

- Claude: In the [Connectors directory](https://claude.ai/customize/connectors), select Add, then Add custom connector. Enter a name and your server's URL, then select Continue. On Team and Enterprise plans, an Owner adds custom connectors for the organization. See [Add a connector that isn't in the directory](https://claude.com/docs/connectors/custom/add-unlisted#add-a-connector-by-url).
- ChatGPT: In [ChatGPT Plugins](https://chatgpt.com/plugins), select the plus button, then Add custom MCP server. Enter a name, a description, and your server's URL, configure authentication, then select Create as a plugin. See [Connect and test your plugin](https://developers.openai.com/plugins/deploy/connect-chatgpt).
- Cursor: Add your server's URL to `.cursor/mcp.json`, as described in [Cursor's MCP documentation](https://cursor.com/docs/mcp):

.cursor/mcp.json

```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "server-name": {
      "url": "https://my-mcp-server.vercel.app/api/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

You can now ask the host to roll a die with your `roll_dice` tool.

Connect your deployed MCP server to an agent so the model can discover and call its tools. Use the full Streamable HTTP endpoint, such as `https://my-mcp-server.vercel.app/api/mcp`, when configuring the connection.

Choose the integration for your agent framework:

- [AI SDK](https://vercel.com/docs/mcp/integrations/ai-sdk): Create a client with `createMCPClient` from `@ai-sdk/mcp`, retrieve the server's tools with `client.tools()`, and pass them to your model call. The guide includes a complete example that calls this page's `roll_dice` tool and closes the client when generation finishes.
- [eve](https://vercel.com/docs/mcp/integrations/eve): Define an MCP connection with `defineMcpClientConnection` under `agent/connections/`, using your server's endpoint and a description of its tools. eve discovers the connection from the filesystem. The guide demonstrates OAuth authentication through Vercel Connect using Linear; configure the connector and credentials for your own server when adapting it.
- [TanStack AI](https://vercel.com/docs/mcp/integrations/tanstack-ai): Create a client with `@tanstack/ai-mcp` and pass it to `chat()` through `mcp.clients`. TanStack AI discovers and executes the server's tools, and `connection: 'close'` closes the client when the run ends. The guide uses this page's `roll_dice` tool.

If you enable authorization, configure the agent's MCP connection with credentials your server accepts. Model-provider credentials authenticate model requests separately. For OAuth consent and token management, use [Vercel Connect](https://vercel.com/docs/connect).

After connecting, ask the agent to use `roll_dice` to roll a six-sided die. A successful tool call returns a value between one and six.

`mcp-handler` includes helpers for verifying bearer tokens and publishing OAuth protected resource metadata. You provide an authorization server and the logic that validates its tokens. The package does not issue tokens or run an authorization server.

MCP clients also need a way to register with your authorization server. The [MCP specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/authorization/client-registration) recommends Client ID Metadata Documents, with Dynamic Client Registration as a fallback, so check that your authorization server supports at least one of them.

Wrap your MCP handler with `withMcpAuth` and set `required: true` to require a valid token. Return the verified client's identity and scopes from `verifyToken`.

The following example uses a token from the `MCP_DEMO_TOKEN` environment variable for local testing. Set that variable in `.env.local` before starting your development server. For production, replace the comparison with your authorization server's token verification, including issuer, audience, expiration, and granted scopes.

With this configuration, requests without a valid token receive `401`. If a verified token lacks a required scope, the handler returns `403`.

To comply with the MCP specification, your server must expose a [metadata endpoint](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/authorization/authorization-server-discovery) that provides OAuth configuration details. Among other things, this endpoint allows MCP clients to discover how to authorize with your server, which authorization servers can issue valid tokens, and what scopes are supported.

4. Replace the `https://example-authorization-server-issuer.com` URL with your own [Authorization Server (AS) Issuer URL](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9728#name-protected-resource-metadata).
5. Set `resourceUrl` to the public URL of your MCP route, including `/api/mcp`.

To view the full list of values available to be returned in the OAuth Protected Resource Metadata JSON, see the protected resource metadata [RFC](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9728#name-protected-resource-metadata).

MCP clients that are compliant with the latest version of the MCP spec can now securely connect and invoke tools defined in your MCP server, when provided with a valid OAuth token.

Each request to your MCP route runs in a [Vercel Function](https://vercel.com/docs/functions), so the function's maximum duration limits each tool call. With [Fluid compute](https://vercel.com/docs/fluid-compute), the default is 300 seconds on every plan. Hobby allows up to 300 seconds. Pro and Enterprise allow up to 800 seconds, or 1,800 seconds with the [extended max duration beta](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/configuring-functions/duration#extended-max-duration-beta). To raise the limit, export `maxDuration` from `app/api/mcp/route.ts`. For longer jobs, have the tool start a [Vercel Workflow](https://vercel.com/docs/workflows) and return the run ID, then add a second tool that reports the run's status.

Your MCP route uses standard [Vercel Functions pricing](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/usage-and-pricing). MCP traffic tends to arrive in short bursts separated by long idle periods. With [Fluid compute](https://vercel.com/docs/fluid-compute), one function instance can handle several requests at once. Active CPU billing pauses while your code waits on I/O, such as a model response or a database query, and provisioned memory is billed while the instance runs. If your tools call models through [AI Gateway](https://vercel.com/docs/ai-gateway/pricing), you pay the provider's list price for tokens, with no AI Gateway markup.

Yes. `createMcpHandler` returns a Web-standard handler that accepts a `Request` and returns a `Response`, so it doesn't depend on Next.js or Vercel. You can mount it in a Nuxt or Nitro server handler with `fromWebHandler` from `h3`, in a SvelteKit server route, or in a Hono route by passing `c.req.raw`. Frameworks built on Node.js `IncomingMessage` and `ServerResponse`, such as Express, need an adapter that creates a Web `Request`. The `/api/mcp` path is a convention. `mcp-handler` doesn't read the request path, so you can mount it at any route and give clients that route's full URL.

Yes, if you run that code in [Vercel Sandbox](https://vercel.com/docs/sandbox) instead of your function. Each sandbox is a Firecracker microVM with its own filesystem and network, and the default image includes Node.js and Python. A tool can create a sandbox with `@vercel/sandbox`, run a command, and return a short summary to the model instead of the raw output. On Vercel, the Sandbox SDK authenticates with your project's OIDC token, so you don't add another credential. A sandbox times out after 5 minutes by default, and you can extend it to 45 minutes on Hobby or 24 hours on Pro and Enterprise. For a complete example, [build a data analysis MCP server with Sandbox](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/large-scale-data-analysis-vercel-sandbox-mcp) that runs DuckDB SQL and Python against large datasets.

Combine authorization with Vercel's network controls:

- Wrap your handler with `withMcpAuth` and `required: true`, as shown in Enabling authorization. Requests without a valid token receive `401`, and tokens without a required scope receive `403`.
- Add a [WAF rate limiting rule](https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-firewall/vercel-waf/rate-limiting) for your MCP path, or call `checkRateLimit` from `@vercel/firewall` in the route with the [rate limiting SDK](https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-firewall/vercel-waf/rate-limiting-sdk).
- Keep [Deployment Protection](https://vercel.com/docs/deployment-protection) on preview deployments. To test a protected preview from an MCP client, send your project's [automation bypass secret](https://vercel.com/docs/deployment-protection/methods-to-bypass-deployment-protection/protection-bypass-automation) in the `x-vercel-protection-bypass` header.

Learn how to deploy MCP servers on Vercel, connect to them using the AI SDK, and explore curated lists of public MCP servers.
